system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2170-09-25 17:43:00 to 2170-10-03 19:52:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman was admitted for acute worsening of chronic lower extremity lymphedema over 2.5 weeks, with significant swelling, weight gain, and discomfort. She was treated with IV furosemide via an existing PICC line, fluid and sodium restriction, and compression. Imaging confirmed no DVT, and her heart function remained stable. The hospital course was complicated by a catheter-associated UTI with Citrobacter freundii, treated with ciprofloxacin. Diuresis was limited by a rise in creatinine to 1.5, prompting transition back to oral bumetanide. Oral thrush and a candidal rash under the breast were treated with nystatin and miconazole. Her INR was optimized to 2.6 on warfarin 9mg daily. She improved clinically, with reduced edema and stable symptoms, and was discharged home on antibiotics, diuretics, and anticoagulation, with strong recommendations to follow up with primary care and a lymphedema clinic.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Infection and inflammatory reaction due to indwelling urinary catheter
Urinary catheterization as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure
Other diuretics causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

Ms ___-

You were admitted to ___ for worsening cellulitis and an 
approximate 20 lb weight gain. You were given IV antibiotics for 
your infection, and were given an IV medication to help you 
urinate off the extra fluid. At discharge, your weight is 348 
lbs.

Please take all your medications as prescribed, Weigh yourself 
every morning, and attend all your follow up appointments as 
described below. Please also continue home ___ for wound care 
and medication management.

It was a pleasure being part of your care, and we wish you the 
best in the future- 

-Your ___ Care Team
 
Followup Instructions:
___

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I fell at home while cleaning the floor. Landed on my right leg. Since then, it’s gotten really red, warm, and swollen—more than usual. I’ve had this before, like cellulitis flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever. Just the leg pain and my back acting up again. And I’ve gained weight—up to 352 pounds. I can barely walk now, feels like I’m carrying fluid on my legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll check your vitals and get some labs. Your breathing has a bit of wheeze, but you’re not short of breath. We’ll also do a chest X-ray to make sure the fluid isn’t in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ve been using my walker more because of the swelling. Normally I just use a cane.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is back. No signs of fluid in the lungs, which is good. But your white blood cell count is high—15.2—suggesting infection in your leg. We’ll start IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on doxycycline for years to prevent these flares. Why isn’t it working now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes bacteria become resistant, or the infection is more severe. We’re starting vancomycin because it covers more types of bacteria, especially since you’re on long-term doxycycline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the swelling? I feel so heavy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve gained nearly 20 pounds since your last dry weight. We think it’s due to your heart not relaxing properly—diastolic dysfunction. We’ll start IV furosemide twice a day to help you pass the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s heart-related? But I’m not short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Some people feel it mostly in their legs. The heart isn’t filling well, so fluid backs up. Your proBNP is only 110, which is mild, but your exam and weight gain support this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve started to urinate more—great sign. We’re seeing good diuresis. Your creatinine was 1.4 yesterday, so we’re watching your kidneys closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? My kidneys were an issue last time I was here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s slightly elevated, but stable. We’ll keep the IV lasix but monitor your labs daily. We don’t want to push too hard and hurt your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’ve got these sores in my mouth and a rash where the IV is. Could it be from the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Vancomycin can cause skin reactions and mouth ulcers in some people. We’ll stop it and switch to clindamycin, which also treats your cellulitis but is gentler on your skin and mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. The mouth sores are really painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you nystatin mouthwash to soothe the ulcers. Swish and spit four times a day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—13.2 today. That means the antibiotics are working. You’ve also lost about 5 pounds—great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit lighter. Can I walk more now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can try with assistance. Keep using the walker. The redness in your leg is improving, but it’s still tender. No pus or spreading, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about going home. I live alone, and my aide was gone for a week. She said I looked really swollen when she came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re arranging home health services. A nurse will check your leg, help with meds, and monitor your weight daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. And my warfarin? I’m on 6 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing warfarin. No issues with your INR so far. You have a history of DVT and PE, so staying on it is crucial.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re down to 348 pounds—close to your target. Creatinine improved to 1.2. We’ll switch you to oral bumetanide at 3 mg twice a day when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was only taking 2 mg a few times a week before. Is 3 mg twice a day safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll monitor your potassium. You’re on spironolactone and potassium supplements, so we’ll check levels with your outpatient labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth feels better with the nystatin. Should I keep using it after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use it as needed for pain. It’s not an antibiotic, just helps soothe the sores. Stop when you’re comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg is less red and warm. WBC is stable. You’re making great progress. We’ll keep clindamycin IV for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need IV antibiotics at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for about a week. Home health will bring the IV meds and teach you or your aide how to give them safely through your PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still using my albuterol inhaler sometimes. Is my lung issue related to all this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have chronic airway obstruction, likely from obesity and possibly asthma. The wheezing isn’t worse, so we’ll keep your inhalers as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge in a couple of days. You’re close to your weight goal, infection is improving, and you’re moving better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain 3 pounds in a day or 5 in a week, call your doctor. Watch for increased leg redness, fever, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on topiramate and levetiracetam for years. Any changes there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. You have seizure disorder and non-epileptic events. Keep taking both meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are good. Creatinine 1.2, potassium 3.6. We’ll keep your diuretics and continue clindamycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my thyroid? I take levothyroxine daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue 50 mcg daily. No signs of under- or overactive thyroid. We’ll check TSH at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using morphine and oxycontin for pain. Is that okay long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have chronic back and leg pain. These are appropriate for now. Just take them as prescribed and avoid alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s weight was 348 pounds—perfect. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning if all stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue warfarin, spironolactone, bumetanide 3 mg twice a day, and your seizure meds. Clindamycin IV for a week, plus nystatin for mouth sores as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another PICC line flush?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re sending you home with saline and heparin flushes. Home health will help with that to keep the line working and prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I should lose weight. Any advice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Focus on small steps. Low-sodium diet, daily weights, and staying active as you can. Your PCP can refer you to nutrition and lymphedema clinics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. Your infection and fluid overload are much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What’s the plan for follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary doctor in a week. They’ll check your INR and chemistry panel. Home health will visit three times this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my leg? Should I keep it elevated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, elevate when sitting. Wear compression if you can tolerate it. Watch for redness or warmth returning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The discharge team will bring your instructions and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep using your EpiPen if you have a severe allergic reaction. And avoid NSAIDs and aspirin—they’re on your allergy list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I know. I use acetaminophen instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s much safer with your warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my CPAP? I don’t use it much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try to use it nightly. Sleep apnea makes heart strain worse. Your PCP can help troubleshoot comfort issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll give it another try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all for now. Rest up, and we’ll get you home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The nurse will be in shortly to assist with discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your esomeprazole for GERD. Keep taking it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t missed a dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That helps protect your stomach, especially with the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll let the team know you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay well.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman was admitted for worsening right leg cellulitis and acute-on-chronic volume overload following a fall at home. She presented with increased leg redness, warmth, and swelling, along with a 14-pound weight gain. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis, and a chest X-ray ruled out pulmonary congestion. She was treated with IV furosemide for diastolic heart failure, achieving significant diuresis and weight reduction to 348 pounds. Vancomycin was initiated for cellulitis but switched to clindamycin due to skin sloughing and oral ulcerations. Home IV antibiotics, increased oral diuretic therapy with bumetanide, and continued management of chronic conditions including anticoagulation, seizure disorder, and hypothyroidism were arranged. She improved clinically, with reduced infection signs and better mobility, and was discharged home with home health services for wound care, medication administration, and monitoring.
